Preparation of IL-12-AMCA-DSPE and IL-12-Cp-DSPE
To visualize the IL-12 anchorage on RBC in vitro and in situ retention of IL/aC@RBAH in vivo, IL-12 was respectively labeled with AMCA and Cypate. Briefly, AMCA (2.00 mg, 8.58 μmol) or Cypate (5.32 mg, 8.58 μmol) was dissolved in DMSO (100 μL). Then, NHS (1.19 mg, 10.30 μmol) and EDCI (1.97 mg, 10.30 μmol) were added and reacted at room temperature for 2 h to afford activated AMCA or Cypate. Subsequently, 5 mg of IL-12 was added into carbonate buffer solution at pH 9.2 (250 μL) and mixed with 25 μL of activated AMCA/Cypate. After stirring in dark overnight at 4 °C, the as-prepared IL-12-AMCA and IL-12-Cp were respectively ultrafiltered (3.5 kD molecular weight cut off (MWCO)), Millipore Sigma) to clear away the free AMCA/Cypate. Subsequently, IL-12-AMCA or IL-12-Cp was mixed with sulfo-SMCC (33 μg, 0.075 μmol) in PBS for 2 h, and further ultrafiltered (3.5 kD MWCO, Millipore Sigma) to afford Mal-IL-12-AMCA or Mal-IL-12-Cp.
5 mg of DSPE-PEG2000-SH was dissolved in DMSO (50 μL) and Mal-IL-12-AMCA or Mal-IL-12-Cp was dissolved in PBS (500 μL). 1.8 μL of DSPE-PEG2000-SH was subsequently added into Mal-IL-12-AMCA or Mal-IL-12-Cp solution and stirred at room temperature for 2 h. Finally, the resultant DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12-AMCA or DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12-Cp product was concentrated via ultrafiltration (3.5 kD MWCO, Millipore Sigma) and stored at 4 °C for use.

Preparation of aCTLA-4-FITC
100 μg of aCTLA-4 was dissolved in Na2CO3-NaHCO3 buffer at pH 9.0 (0.1 M, 100 μL). After 10 min of stirring at 4 °C, 1.03 μg of FITC was added and further stirred at 4 °C for 18 h. Finally, NH4Cl (5 M, 1 μL) was added to cease the reaction. Free FITC was removed by ultrafiltration (3.0 kD molecular weight cutoff (MWCO), Millipore Sigma) with the endpoint as determined by the visual clarity of the filtrate.

Preparation of IL/aC@RBC
aC@RBC was prepared via an optimized “alternate hypotonic and hypertonic dialysis” approach as reported71. Briefly, the whole blood was collected from healthy BALB/c mice and mixed with PBS buffer with 5% EDTA. The obtained RBC was isolated by centrifugation (800×g, 4 °C, 5 min) three times and resuspended in PBS buffer at 70% hematocrit. Then 500 μL of RBC suspension and 85 μL of FITC labeled aCTLA-4 (aCTLA-4-FITC, 5 mg/mL) were mixed and dialyzed (3.5 kD MWCO) against 40 mL of hypotonic buffer (deionized water containing 10 mM NaHCO3, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 20 mM glucose, 2 mM ATP, and 3 mM reduced glutathione (GSH)) at 4 °C for 90 min. Subsequently, the buffer was replaced with 45 mL of PBS buffer for 5 min of balance and then dialyzed with 50 mL of hypertonic buffer containing 10% PIGPA-NaCl buffer (deionized water containing 100 mM sodium pyruvate, 100 mM inosine, 100 mM glucose, 33 mM NaH2PO4, 12% (w/v) NaCl, and 2 mM ATP, pH 7.4) at 37 °C for 30 min. The resealed aC@RBC was collected by centrifugation (1000×g, 4 °C, 10 min) and washed 3 times with PBS buffer to remove unentrapped aCTLA-4.
For efficient IL-12 anchorage and aCTLA-4 encapsulation in RBC for IL/aC@RBC, the loading capacities were investigated by varying the feeding time points of aCTLA-4.
IL/aC@RBC-1 was synthesized as follows: 500 μL of RBC suspension (4×109/mL), 85 μL of aCTLA-4-FITC (5 mg/mL), and 100 μL of DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12-AMCA (5 mg/mL) were mixed, and then dialyzed (3.5 kD MWCO) against 40 mL of hypotonic buffer. Subsequently, the buffer was replaced with 35 mL of PBS buffer for balance and then dialyzed with 50 mL of hypertonic buffer for further 30 min. The resealed IL/aC@RBC was collected by centrifugation (1000×g, 4 °C, 10 min) and washed 3 times with PBS buffer to remove unentrapped aCTLA-4-FITC and DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12.
IL/aC@RBC-2 was synthesized as follows: 500 μL of RBC suspension (4×109/mL) was mixed with 85 μL of aCTLA-4-FITC (5 mg/mL) and then dialyzed (3.5 kD MWCO) against 40 mL of hypotonic buffer. Subsequently, the buffer was substituted with 35 mL of PBS buffer for balance. The resultant aC@RBC was added with 100 μL of DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12-AMCA (5 mg/mL) and dialyzed by 50 mL of hypertonic buffer. The resealed IL/aC@RBC was collected by centrifugation (1000×g, 4 °C, 10 min) and washed 3 times with PBS buffer to remove unentrapped aCTLA-4-FITC and DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12.
IL/aC@RBC-3 was synthesized as follows: 500 μL of RBC suspension (4×109/mL) and 85 μL of aCTLA-4-FITC (5 mg/mL) were mixed and then dialyzed (3.5 kD MWCO) against 40 mL of hypotonic buffer. Subsequently, the buffer was substituted with 35 mL of PBS buffer for balance and then dialyzed by 40 mL of hypertonic buffer. The resealed aC@RBC was collected by centrifugation (1000×g, 4 °C, 10 min) and washed 3 times with PBS buffer to remove unentrapped aCTLA-4-FITC. Then the resultant aC@RBC was added with 100 μL of IL-12-AMCA-DSPE (5 mg/mL) and incubated in PBS for IL-12 intercalation at 37 °C. The engineered IL/aC@RBC was collected by centrifugation (1000×g, 4 °C, 10 min) and washed 3 times with PBS buffer to remove unentrapped DSPE-PEG2000-IL-12.

In vitro bioactivity assessment of Catalase (CAT) and IL-12
For CAT bioactivity evaluation, native RBC (nRBC) and RBC membrane (RBCM) were extracted as previous studies. Briefly, the whole blood was harvested from healthy BALB/c mice, collected in a tube, and then centrifuged (800×g, 4 °C, 5 min) to discard plasma, leukocytes, and platelets in the upper layers. The precipitates were resuspended and washed three times by pre-cooled PBS buffer for nRBC. The resultant nRBC was diluted 40 times by pre-cooled lysate (0.01 M Tris-HCl, pH 8.0) containing 0.02 mM PMSF and stood at 4 °C for 2 h. Subsequently, RBCM was obtained by centrifugation (10,000×g, 4 °C, 30 min), washed three times, and stored at −80 °C for further use. RBC and IL/aC@RBC were prepared via the optimized “alternate hypotonic and hypertonic dialysis” approach as introduced in “preparation of IL/aC@RBC”. Finally, the catalase bioactivities of nRBC, RBC, RBCM, and IL/aC@RBC were respectively assessed by Catalase Assay Kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China), and normalized by the whole protein in the samples. In addition, the O2 generation from IL/aC@RBC and native RBC (nRBC) were quantitatively investigated to affirm CAT reservation on IL/aC@RBC. Briefly, 109 cells of IL/aC@RBC and nRBC were respectively dispersed in 5 mL of PBS buffer containing 500 μM H2O2. Then, the changes in O2 concentration were determined in 2 min by a dissolved oxygen analyzer.
For IL-12 bioactivity assessment, splenocytes were extracted for the evaluation of IFN-γ production stimulated by free IL-12 and IL@RBC. Briefly, spleens were collected from healthy BALB/c mice. The splenocytes were extracted and processed to remove RBC by lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The obtained cells were seeded in a 96-well plate and subjected to free IL-12 or IL@RBC at pre-designated concentrations at 37 °C for 48 h. The culture supernatants were respectively collected for IFN-γ evaluation by ELISA (Mouse IFN-γ ELISA, Elabscience), and normalized by the whole protein in the samples.

Preparation of BaO2
Polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP, 0.35 g, 6.03 μmol) was ultrasonically dissolved in 15 mL of methanol, followed by the addition of BaCl2 (0.1 g, 0.48 mmol) and further stirring for complete dissolution. Then 20 μL of choline hydroxide (44% wt) was added to the solution. After 30 min of reaction, the mixture was dripped with 6 mL of 3% H2O2 at a constant rate of 0.05 mL/min and then stirred at room temperature for 1 h. The resultant BaO2 products were collected by centrifugation (10,000×g, 4 °C, 15 min). After discarding the supernatant, the precipitates were resuspended by 15 mL of methanol and washed three times to afford white precipitates for further use.

Determination of Ba2+ and H2O2 generation from BaO2
In vitro release of Ba2+ from BaO2 was measured using the dialysis bag diffusion method. Typically, 1 mg of BaO2 nanoparticles in 1 mL of PBS (pH 7.4) were respectively dialyzed (1 kD MWCO) against 19 mL of PBS at pH 7.4 and pH 6.5. The dialysis was performed at 37 °C with a shaking speed of 100 rpm. At pre-designed time points of 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h, 1 mL of dialysate was collected and replaced with 1 mL of fresh medium. The obtained samples were diluted with 3% HNO3 and the Ba2+ concentration was quantified by Inductively Coupled Plasma-Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS, iCAP RQplus, Thermo Scientific, USA).
To evaluate the acidity-induced generation of H2O2, 100 μL of BaO2 nanoparticles (0.1 mg/mL) was incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) in 1.5 mL of PBS at pH 7.4 and pH 6.5, respectively. At pre-designed time points of 0, 4, 10, 20, and 30 min, 200 μL of tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) was added for 2–3 min of incubation. The absorption at 652 nm was measured by UV–vis spectrophotometer (3J1-0015, HITACHI, Japan) and H2O2 production was calculated according to the established standard curve of commercial H2O2 (0.05-1.0 mM).

Rheological test
Rheological characterizations of IL/aC@RBAH were observed using a rheometer (Discovery HR-2-TA, TA Instrument, American) with a parallel-plate geometry of 12 mm diameter and 0.6 mm gap at 25 °C. The changes in storage modulus and loss modulus of IL/aC@RBAH were monitored at a constant strain of 2.5% and a fixed frequency of 1 Hz for 20 min. Strain amplitude sweeps were conducted from (1% to 1000%) at a fixed frequency of 1 Hz. Dynamic oscillatory frequency sweeps were performed from 1 to 32 rad/s at a constant strain of 2.5% to estimate the elastic and viscous properties of IL/aC@RBAH.

In vitro degradation determination of IL/aC@RBAH hydrogel
The degradation profile of IL/aC@RBAH was investigated relying on the mass loss during the degradation process. Typically, BaO2 (0.1 mg), 3% Alg (100 μL), and IL/aC@RBC (2×108 cells in 100 μL) were mixed and incubated in PBS at pH 6.5 for IL/aC@RBAH formation. Afterward, the hydrogel was washed by deionized water three times and then dried under vacuum at −40 °C for 4–6 h. The initial mass of lyophilized IL/aC@RBAH was indicated as W0. Subsequently, the lyophilized IL/aC@RBAH was swollen in PBS at pH 6.5 and incubated at 37 °C. At designated time points on the 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 14 days, the hydrogel was collected, dried, and weighed (Wd). The degradation percentage (D%) of IL/aC@RBAH was calculated according to the formula as follows:
D(%) = (W0 - Wd) / W0 × 100%

Release of IL-12, aCTLA-4 and Ba2+ from IL/aC@RBAH
IL-12 and aCTLA-4 in IL/aC@RBAH were respectively labeled with AMCA and FITC to obtain IL-12-AMCA and aCTLA-4-FITC. The release behaviors of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 were examined according to the previous report72. A 40 µm cell strainer containing IL/aC@RBAH was embedded in a six-well plate with 5 mL of PBS at pH 6.5 and pH 7.4. After 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 16, 24, and 48 h of incubation, the concentrations of IL-12-AMCA and aCTLA-4-FITC in PBS were respectively detected by a microplate reader (Molecular Devices, USA) at the absorption wavelength of 350 nm and 488 nm.
In vitro release of Ba2+ from IL/aC@RBAH was investigated via the dialysis method. Briefly, IL/aC@RBAH formed in PBS (pH 6.5) was washed with deionized water three times, and then 1 mL of the sample was dialyzed (3 kD MWCO) against 19 mL of PBS (pH 6.5) at 37 °C in a shaking culture incubator. After 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 16, 24, and 48 h of incubation, 1 mL of dialysate was taken and replenished with an equal volume of fresh buffer. The released Ba2+ amount was determined by ICP-MS (iCAP RQplus, Thermo Scientific, USA).

In vitro biosafety evaluation
For the cytotoxicity analysis of BaO2, 4×103 4T1 cells and Panc02 cells were plated in each well of 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Different concentrations of BaO2 (0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, and 150 μg/mL) were added for 24 h of incubation. Afterward, MTT solution (0.5 mg/mL) was added and cocultured at 37 °C for 4 h. Then medium containing MTT was removed and replaced with 150 μL of DMSO in each well. After 30 min of constant temperature shaking at 37 °C, the optical density (OD) at 490 nm was detected. The experiment was repeated independently 5 times and the cell viability was calculated according to the formula: cell viability (%) = ODsample / ODcontrol × 100%.
For the biocompatibility evaluation of IL/aC@RBAH, hydrogel leaching solution was collected and diluted into different concentrations (0, 6.25%, 12.5%, 25%, 50%, and 100%). 4T1 cells and Panc02 cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C. After 24 h of culture, hydrogel leaching solutions at various concentrations were added and cocultured for 24 h. Subsequently, MTT solution (0.5 mg/mL) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Then medium containing MTT was removed and replaced with 150 μL of DMSO in each well. After 30 min of constant temperature shaking at 37 °C, the OD at 490 nm was detected. The experiment was repeated independently 5 times for statistical analysis.
IL/aC@RBAH cytotoxicity was further investigated by live/dead cell staining assay. Briefly, sterile IL/aC@RBAH was placed in 48-well plates and 1×104 4T1 cells were seeded in the wells containing hydrogels, followed by 24 h of incubation at 37 °C. Subsequently, the cells were stained with calcein-AM (1 μg/mL) and PI (1 μg/mL) for confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM, Olympus Corporation, Japan) observation.

Colony formation assay
The cell viability exposed to different treatments was investigated via colony formation assay. Typically, one hundred cells were seeded in culture dishes (60 mm in diameter) and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Subsequently, cells were respectively subjected to saline, RT, RT+BaO2, RT+IL/aC@RBC, and RT+IL/aC@RB. The X-ray irradiation intensity was 1 Gy. Then cells were incubated for 14 days and replaced with fresh culture medium every 2–3 days. After colony formation in each dish, the cells were washed with PBS several times and fixed by 4% polyformaldehyde for 30 min at room temperature. Finally, colonies were dyed with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min and washed by PBS for visual observation. The colonies were counted and calculated for survival fraction analysis.

Detection of intracellular ROS production
The ROS production inside cells was investigated by Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit (DCFH-DA, ROS fluorescence probe). 4T1 cells were cultured in confocal dishes and 12-well plates for 24 h at 37 °C and then added with DCFH-DA solution (10 μM). Subsequently, cells were treated with saline, RT, RT+BaO2, RT+IL/aC@RBC, and RT+IL/aC@RB, respectively cells and then incubated with DCFH-DA solution (10 μM) for 20 min at 37 °C. Afterward, the cells in 12-well plates were trypsinized and collected for flow cytometry. Meanwhile, the cells in confocal dishes were washed and stained with DAPI for observation by CLSM (Olympus Corporation, Japan).

In vivo degradation tests and in situ retention tests
In vivo degradation tests: The mixture of Ba2+, IL/aC@RBC, and Alg was injected into the right thorax of female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=3 mice per group). On days 7 and 14 after in situ administration, a small incision of about 1 cm was created on the injected site, and the residual hydrogel was photographed.
In situ retention tests: For real-time monitoring of in situ retention of IL/aC@RBAH in female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=3 mice per group), the IL-12 was pre-labeled by Cypate for IL-Cp&aC, IL-Cp/aC@RBC, and IL-Cp/aC@RBAH. At 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 14 days after subcutaneous injection and intratumoral injection, the fluorescence intensities were monitored by the IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS Lumina XR, USA).

In vivo safety analysis
For cytokine analysis of serum, the orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were intratumorally injected with saline, IL-12, aCTLA-4, and IL/aC@RBAH (n=3 mice per group), respectively. After 4 h, the blood samples were collected and centrifuged (800×g, 4 °C, 10 min) to remove cells. The concentrations of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 in the serum samples were determined by IL-12 and aCTLA-4 ELISA kit, and measured by microplate reader (Molecular Devices, USA).
For blood biochemical analysis, the orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were intratumorally injected with saline, IL/aC, RBAH, and IL/aC@RBAH (n=3 mice per group), respectively. After 3 days, the blood samples were acquired for quiescence at 4 °C overnight and further centrifugation (800×g, 4 °C, 10 min) to remove cells. The serum samples were collected and sent to Servicebio Biotechnology Co., Ltd for analysis of liver function (Aspartate aminotransferase, ALT; Alanine aminotransferase, AST) and renal function (Creatinine, CREA; Blood urea nitrogen, BUN). The major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) from the mice subjected to different treatments were collected for H&E staining analysis.
For long-term biosafety analysis, healthy BALB/c mice were randomly allocated into 4 groups (n=3 mice per group) and subcutaneously injected with saline, IL&aC (the mixture of IL-12 and aCTLA-4), RB (the mixture of RBC and BaO2), and IL/aC@RBAH once a week. During 2 months of continuous treatments, the body weights of the mice were recorded every 7 days. After 2 months of monitoring, the blood and major organs were collected. Liver damage indexes involving alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), as well as kidney function indexes compromising blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine (CREA), were respectively detected. In addition, the major organs, including heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney, were collected for H&E analysis.

Evaluation of intratumoral oxygen contents
The female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=3 mice per group) were orthotopically inoculated with 4T1 cells (1×106 cells per mouse) to establish a 4T1 mouse breast tumor model. When the tumor volume reached approximately 100 mm3, the mice were subjected to treatments of IL/aC@RBC or IL/aC@RB. For quantification of intratumoral vascular oxygen saturation levels, the ratios of deoxygenated hemoglobin (λ=750 nm) versus oxygenated hemoglobin (λ=850 nm) were recorded, and the 2D photoacoustic (PA) images were monitored by PA imaging system (Vevo® LAZR, Fujifilm VisualSonics, Canada). In addition, for oxygen production sustainability evaluation, the orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were respectively treated with IL/aC@RB and IL/aC@RBAH. At 0, 24, and 48 h post-treatment, the tumors were photographed by PA imaging system (Vevo® LAZR, Fujifilm VisualSonics, Canada) and the intratumoral vascular oxygen saturation levels were recorded.
For further evaluation of the intratumoral hypoxia relief, the orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=3 mice per group) were respectively treated with saline, BaO2, IL/aC@RBC, IL/aC@RB, and IL/aC@RBAH. After 24 h, animals were sacrificed, and the tumors were collected. Subsequently, these tissues were successively frozen, sectioned, air-dried, fixed in acetone, and blocked. Immunofluorescence staining of HIF-1α and CD31 was conducted and then observed by CLSM (Olympus Corporation, Japan).

In vivo antitumor study on 4T1 tumor models and Panc02 tumor models
For orthotopic 4T1 tumor therapy, 1×106 4T1 expressing luciferase (4T1-luc) cells were injected into the left mammary fat pad of female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=5 mice per group). After the tumor volume reached 100 mm3, the mice were randomly divided into 6 groups (5 mice per group) and respectively treated with saline (G1), RT (G2), RT+RBAH (G3), RT+aC@RBAH (G4), RT+IL@RBAH (G5), and RT+IL/aC@RBAH (G6) (an equivalent aCTLA-4 amount of 500 μg/kg, IL-12 amount of 250 μg/kg, BaO2 amount of 150 μg/kg, and Alg amount of 3%). The X-ray irradiation treatment (8 Gy) in the pre-designed groups was imposed twice at the tumor sites after 0 and 2 days of in situ administration. On the 7, 14, and 21 days after the tumor inoculation, the tumor growth was monitored by the IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS Lumina XR, USA). The tumor sizes and body weight were recorded every 2 days. The survival of mice was monitored over a 2-month period. The tumor volume (V) was calculated following the formula V=0.5×W2×L, where L represents the long diameter of the tumor and W represents the width of the tumor. The tumors from the mice were collected for histological analysis, including H&E staining and Ki67 staining.
For evaluating the antitumor efficacy of RT+IL/aC@RBAH-induced multistage RIT, an orthotopic 4T1 tumor model was established. After the tumor volume reached 100 mm3, the female BALB/c mice were randomly divided into 6 groups (6–8 weeks old, n=5 mice per group) and respectively treated with saline, RT, RT+RBAH, IL&aC, RT+IL&aC, and RT+IL/aC@RBAH (an equivalent aCTLA-4 amount of 500 μg/kg, IL-12 amount of 250 μg/kg, BaO2 amount of 150 μg/kg, and Alg amount of 3%). The X-ray irradiation treatment (8 Gy) in the pre-designed groups was imposed twice at the tumor sites after 0 and 2 days of in situ administration. On the 7, 14, and 21 days after the tumor inoculation, the tumor growth was monitored by the IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System. The tumor sizes and survival time were also recorded. The tumor volume (V) was calculated following the formula V=0.5×W2×L.
For orthotopic 4T1 tumor relapse, 1×106 4T1 cells were injected into the left mammary fat pad of female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old, n=5 mice per group). After 10 days, the mice were treated with RT+IL/aC@RBAH. Following 2 more days, the mice were re-treated with RT. On day 26, the mice presenting CR after RT+IL/aC@RBAH treatment were rechallenged with 1×106 4T1 cells into the right mammary fat pad. Meanwhile, healthy mice were orthotopically injected with 1×106 4T1 cells into the right flank of mice as the control. The tumor growth was tracked every 2 days and calculated following the formula V=0.5×W2×L.
For comparing the antitumor efficacy between RT+aPD-1/aPD-L1 and RT+IL/aC@RBAH, an orthotopic 4T1 tumor model was established in female BALB/c mice. After the tumor volume reached 100 mm3, the mice were randomly divided into 4 groups (6–8 weeks old, n=5 mice per group) and respectively treated with saline, RT+aPD-1 (10 mg/kg), RT+aPD-L1 (10 mg/kg), and RT+IL/aC@RBAH. The X-ray irradiation treatment (8 Gy) in the pre-designed groups was imposed twice at the tumor sites after 0 and 2 days of in situ administration. On the 7, 14, and 21 days after the tumor inoculation, the tumor growth was monitored by the IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System. The tumor growth was tracked every 2 days and calculated following the formula V=0.5×W2×L.
For subcutaneous Panc02 tumor treatment, 1×106 Panc02 cells were injected into the right back of male C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, n=5 mice per group). When subcutaneous tumor volume reached approximately 100 mm3, the mice were subjected to different treatments as designed in the orthotopic 4T1 tumor therapy. On days 7, 14, and 21 after the tumor inoculation, the tumor growth was monitored in real-time by the IVIS Spectrum In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS Lumina XR, USA). The tumor sizes and survival time were also tracked every 2 days. The tumors were taken for histological analysis, including H&E staining and TUNEL staining.

In vivo antitumor immune response analysis
For localized and systemic immune response analysis, orthotopic 4T1 tumor models were established in female BALB/c mice, and subcutaneous Panc02 tumor models were established in male C57BL/6 mice. When the tumors reached approximately 100 mm3, the mice were randomly divided into 6 groups (n=3 mice per group) and treated with saline, RT, RT+RBAH, RT+aC@RBAH, RT+IL@RBAH, and RT+IL/aC@RBAH, respectively. Tumors and TDLNs were both collected 4 days after different treatments. The tissues were rinsed by PBS, minced and digested by Hank’s buffer containing DNase (0.1 mg/mL) and collagenase (1 mg/mL) for 45 min at 37 °C. Then the cells were filtered through 70 μm nylon cell strainers and centrifuged (500×g, 4 °C, 5 min) to obtain single-cell suspensions. Afterward, 1 mL of erythrocyte lysate was added to each sample and lysed for 3 min at room temperature. Then, the cells were washed, blocked by anti-CD16/32 antibody for 5 min and stained with fixable viability stain 510 for 15 min at room temperature. Subsequently, fluorescein-labeled antibodies were added and incubated at 4 °C for 30 min, followed by washing with PBS. For the intracellular staining, the cell suspension was fixed and permeabilized by the fixation/permeabilization buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Then the processed cells were stained with intracellular fluorescein-labeled antibodies and detected by flow cytometry.
For multistage immune effect analysis, the immune cell populations in orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice exposed to different treatments were investigated. Briefly, the orthotopic 4T1-tumor bearing female BALB/c mice were randomly divided into 5 groups (n=3 mice per group) and then respectively treated with saline, RT, RT+IL-aC (IL-12 prior to aCTLA-4), RT+IL&aC (the mixture of IL-12 and aCTLA-4), and RT+aC-IL (IL-12 subsequent to aCTLA-4). Tumors and TDLNs were collected at 4 days after different treatments. The samples were processed as described above. Afterward, the processed cells were stained with intracellular fluorescein-labeled antibodies and detected by flow cytometry.
To further elucidate the antitumor efficacy between RT+IL&aC and RT+IL/aC@RBAH, the immune cell populations in orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing female BALB/c mice exposed to different treatments were investigated. Briefly, the orthotopic 4T1-tumor bearing mice were randomly divided into 3 groups (n=3 mice per group) and then respectively treated with saline, RT+IL&aC, and RT+IL/aC@RBAH. The tumors were collected at 4 days after different treatments. The samples were processed as described above. Subsequently, the processed cells were stained with intracellular fluorescein-labeled antibodies and detected by flow cytometry.
For long-term immune memory evaluation, the orthotopic 4T1 rechallenge model was established as designed above. Briefly, 1×106 4T1 cells were injected into the left mammary fat pad of female BALB/c mice (n=3 mice per group). After 10 days, the mice were treated with RT+IL/aC@RBAH. The X-ray irradiation treatment (8 Gy) was imposed twice at the tumor sites after 0 and 2 days of the treatment. On day 26, the mice presenting CR after RT+IL/aC@RBAH treatment were rechallenged with 1×106 4T1 cells into the right mammary fat pad. Meanwhile, healthy mice were orthotopically injected with 1×106 4T1 cells into the right flank of mice as the control. On day 52, the spleens were collected and processed as above for analysis by flow cytometry.
To compare the antitumor efficacy between RT+aPD-1/aPD-L1 and RT+IL/aC@RBAH, the immune cell populations in orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing female BALB/c mice exposed to different treatments were investigated. Briefly, the orthotopic 4T1-tumor bearing mice were randomly divided into 4 groups (n=3 mice per group) and then respectively treated with saline, RT+aPD-1 (10 mg/kg), RT+aPD-L1 (10 mg/kg), and RT+IL/aC@RBAH. The tumors and TDLNs were collected at 4 days after different treatments. The samples were processed as described above. Afterward, the processed cells were stained with intracellular fluorescein-labeled antibodies and detected by flow cytometry.

Transcriptome analysis
An orthotopic 4T1 tumor model was established for transcriptome analysis. Briefly, 1×106 4T1 cells were injected into the left mammary fat pad of female BALB/c mice. After the tumor size reached 100 mm3, the orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were randomly divided into 3 groups (n=3 mice per group) and exposed to different treatments of saline, RT, and RT+IL/aC@RBAH, respectively. The tumor tissues were harvested on day 3 after treatments. Total RNA was extracted for transcriptome sequencing and analysis containing correlation analysis, differential analysis, GO analysis, KEGG analysis, and GSEA analysis on a Novogene platform (https://magic.novogene.com/).

Statistics and reproducibility
All numeric data are presented as mean ± SD deviation from at least three parallel experiments. No data were excluded from the analyses. The significance between two groups was determined by the two-sided unpaired students’ t-test. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Turkey’s post hoc test was employed for multiple comparisons. Survival analysis was performed by log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v9.5.0). P values of less than 0.05 were considered significant. All flow cytometry data were analyzed on NovoExpress (v1.5.0, Agilent Technologies) and FlowJo software (v10, BD Biosciences). Living imaging software (v4.4, Perkin Elmer) was used to analyse bioluminescent and fluorescent images. Microscopic images were analyzed by Olympus Micro (FV30S-SW) and ImageJ (Version 1.52k). Sex was not considered as a biological variable within each tumor model because 4T1 studies used only female mice and Panc02 studies used only male mice. Therefore, sex-disaggregated analysis within models is not applicable.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I have reviewed the manuscript entitled “Hierarchical brake-releasing and accelerator-pushing butterfly effect of in situ cell reservoir hydrogel for maneuvering multistage radioimmunotherapy”. I have the following comments:
Strengths:
  The paper presents an approach for multistage radioimmunotherapy (RIT) using an in situ cell reservoir hydrogel.
  The hydrogel is composed of red blood cells (RBCs) engineered to carry interleukin-12 (IL-12) and anti-CTLA-4 (aCTLA-4), and barium dioxide (BaO2) for in situ gelation and oxygen production.
  The hydrogel addresses the limitations of radiotherapy (RT) and immunotherapy by:
Improving tumor oxygenation through Ba/O2 dual-compensation.
Sequentially releasing aCTLA-4 to block immune checkpoints and IL-12 to activate immune cells, creating a multistage immune response.
  The approach demonstrates significant antitumor efficacy and improved survival in both 4T1 breast cancer and Panc02 pancreatic cancer models.
  Transcriptomic analysis reveals activation of immune response-related pathways, supporting the multistage immune activation mechanism.
Weaknesses and Suggestions for Improvement:
  The nano material design of hydrogel and RBCs is less innovative, which has been reported a lot. It is unclear why the research focus on CTLA-4 and IL-12, why not PD-1/PD-L1 and other cytokines?
  Mechanism of Action: While the authors propose a mechanism for the multistage immune response, further studies are needed to validate this mechanism. For example, experiments could be conducted to investigate the timing and kinetics of aCTLA-4 and IL-12 release, as well as their respective effects on immune cell populations and function.
  Comparison with Other Therapies: The paper would benefit from a direct comparison with other RT and immunotherapy combinations, including those using different aCTLA-4 and IL-12 formulations and delivery methods. This would provide a clearer understanding of the advantages and limitations of the proposed approach.
  Toxicity and Safety: While the paper mentions that the treatments were well-tolerated and showed no significant toxicity, a more comprehensive assessment of safety is needed. This could include studies on the biodistribution of BaO2 and RBCs, as well as long-term toxicity studies.
  Clinical Translation: The paper should discuss the potential challenges and considerations for clinical translation of the approach, such as the scalability of RBC engineering and the production of BaO2.
Additional Suggestions:
  The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of the potential applications of the approach for different types of cancer.
  The authors could consider exploring the use of other cytokines or immunomodulatory agents in combination with IL-12 and aCTLA-4.
  The paper could be improved by including a more detailed discussion of the economic and logistical considerations for the proposed approach.
Overall, this paper presents a promising approach for multistage RIT with the potential to improve outcomes for cancer patients. Further studies are needed to fully understand the mechanism of action, optimize the treatment regimen, and assess the safety and feasibility for clinical translation.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is a complex study addressing the intrinsic drawbacks of radiotherapy in treating cancer. The authors provided comprehensive in vitro and in vivo data to demonstrate the success of their hydrogel system. Many control groups are included. Overall, this is a well designed study with a good level of innovation.
The title of the paper sounds more like a newspaper article title, instead of a research paper. Lots of concepts are introduced here: e.g.
Hierarchical, "brake-releasing", "accelerator-pushing", "butterfly effect", "double edged sword". None of them are accurate scientific terms. I suggest the authors to revise their title to accurately capture the study results. The schematic in Figure 1 is also too complicated.
I think a good control would be the co-administration of IL12 and CTL4 antibody. Also, many IL12 clinical trials failed due to uncontrolled toxicity in cytokine storm. Can the authors discuss how their system would mitigate this side effect?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Dr. Fan et al. developed an injectable gel encapsulating interleukin-12 and anti-CTLA-4 co-engineered red blood cells. This gel was self-assembled in situ within tumor microenvironments to increase levels of O2, anti-CTLA-4, and IL-12, thereby activating multistage immune responses. While they present an interesting strategy, their approach is quite complex and it is unclear whether this is translationally relevant, especially since they give local injection. I have the following comments.
1. The authors claimed that "In response to the acidic TME, the in situ injected BaO2 undergoes hydrolysis to generate H2O2 and Ba2+, followed by the rapid reaction of Ba2+ with sodium alginate (Alg) to afford a biocompatible hydrogel." However, both in vivo degradation and in situ retention studies were performed on healthy mice (Fig. 4a-c), showing good retention in vivo for up to 14 days. How did the gel form under normal physiological conditions (pH 7.4)? This seemed inconsistent with Fig. 3b and the authors' hypothesis. Moreover, without acid stimulation, how did the system degrade? If BaO2 could decompose under pH 7.4, how to ensure the long-term stability of this gel system?
2. Please plot the gelatin time of the system vs. pH.
3. The authors only mentioned that 500 μL of RBCs was used for the gel system. Then how much O2 could be converted by catalase from these cell mimics? Could the authors provide more detailed preparation and measurement protocols, including the specific amounts of RBCs used and the quantification of O2? A quantitative measurement of O2 generation, rather than enzyme activity, is the key evidence to support the hypothesis.
4. The authors claimed to have used aCTLA-4 but did not indicate its source. They mentioned that PD-L1 (B7-H1) (Cat# BE0101) was purchased from BioXcell, although this study did not utilize it. Please clarify the source of aCTLA-4 and the relevance of PD-L1 in the context of this study. Besides, were the FITC-aCTLA4 get? Please clarify aCLTA-4 ELISA detection kit in serum as the kit was quite rare.
5. Detailed protocols for labeling both IL-12 and aCTLA-4 should be provided. Please also include spectral data (such as NMR, IR, Mass, GPC, etc.) to confirm labeling and modification. A release study in PBS (pH 7.0) is also needed. Additionally, since aCTLA-4 has a molecular weight of 150 kDa, how could it be detected in dialysates from 3 kD MWCO dialysis devices?
6. Did the H2O2 produced by BaO2 hydrolysis and the ROS induced by RT directly damage tumor tissue? If so, what was the killing efficiency, and how does this compare to immune-mediated killing?
7. The authors claimed O2-mediated pore formation in RBC membranes. Please provide direct evidence to support this claim, rather than relying solely on release data, to improve the rigor of the draft. Additionally, will H2O2 and ROS trigger pore formation on the RBC membrane, and how did the authors design the system to avoid this?
8. The authors claimed that there was a sequence of immune actions by the gel system, that ultimately achieved a butterfly effect, a feature of the paper. Please provide more evidence to illustrate this effect, including data on the sequential initiation of the immune response in vivo. Presently, this hypothesis is not consistent with in vivo data. The authors claimed that ‘rapid release of aCTLA-4 to relieve tumor immunosuppression. Subsequently, IL-12 anchored on RBC, acting as a “relay baton”, is dilatorily released and interacts with T/NK cells within the TME to induce IFN-γ-dependent antitumor immunity’. However, in Fig5i-p, comparing G4 and G5, aCTLA-4 alone did not significantly increase T cells, and IL-12 alone also did not significantly increase IFN-γ.
9. Local injection of IL-2 and aCTLA-4 plus RT should be included as a control.
10. Will local RT treatment and/or ROS damage the gel structure? If so, how could cargo burst release be avoided?
11. In Fig. 2b, compared to nRBC, what proteins (MWCO 25 kDa) were lost in RBC? It is necessary to add a set of IL/aC@RBC for comparison.
12. Please provide high-resolution TEM images of the BaO2 products (Fig. S5). It is difficult to conclude that a shortened bamboo-like structure exists for BaO2 here, as well as the particle size distribution.
13. The authors should indicate the gel position in the PA images. Additionally, will the intertumoral-injected gels with cells affect PA imaging? RBC is also rich in O2 and sonification will help O2 release from cell mimics.
14. In Figs. 4l-m, 5f, and 9a, the dense tumor cell nuclei (DAPI staining) showed no signs of reduced tumor cell proliferation following RT+IL/aC@RBAH treatment. Additionally, the HE staining appeared to be collected from the tumor margin.
15. What were the encapsulation efficiency and loading capacity of IL-12 and aCTLA4?
16. For transcriptome analysis, a PBS group is needed as a control.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Detailed responses to the reviewers’ comments
Reviewer #1 (radiosensitization):
“Hierarchical brake-releasing and accelerator-pushing butterfly effect of in situ cell
reservoir hydrogel for maneuvering multistage radioimmunotherapy.” The pain purpose
of this manuscript is to describe a novel hydrogel to potentiate and enhance the effects
of radiation therapy and immunotherapy.
- From a stylistic perspective - there are, in my opinion, too many “buzzwords” and too
much “jargon” in the paper. Words like “strategic” and “hierarchical” are overused and
slightly distracting. The term “butterfly effect” is not well-defined.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s kind suggestion. Considering the scientificity and
preciseness of this article, buzzwords like “strategic” and “hierarchical” have been
removed to straightforward describe our design and results. In our study, the “butterfly
effect” is defined to be multistage immune effects induced by the proposed therapeutic
modality of RT + IL/aC@RBAH. To avert unnecessary confusion, we have substituted
the term “butterfly effect” with “multistage effect” and supplemented relevant
description in the revised manuscript.
- A breast cancer orthotopic model was used to demonstrate the efficacy of the hydrogel.
The same is shown in pancreatic cell models. Overall, this is a well-studied and thought-
provoking model to study the effects of hydrogel on.
Response: Many thanks for the reviewer’s endorsement of our work.
Reviewer #2 (radiosensitization):
I have reviewed the manuscript entitled “Hierarchical brake-releasing and accelerator-
pushing butterfly effect of in situ cell reservoir hydrogel for maneuvering multistage
radioimmunotherapy”. I have the following comments:
Strengths:
The paper presents an approach for multistage radioimmunotherapy (RIT) using an in
situ cell reservoir hydrogel. The hydrogel is composed of red blood cells (RBCs)
engineered to carry interleukin-12 (IL-12), anti-CTLA-4 (aCTLA-4), and barium
dioxide (BaO ) for in situ gelation and oxygen production. The hydrogel addresses the

through Ba/O dual-compensation. Sequentially releasing aCTLA-4 to block immune
2
checkpoints and IL-12 to activate immune cells, creating a multistage immune response.
The approach demonstrates significant antitumor efficacy and improved survival in
both 4T1 breast cancer and Panc02 pancreatic cancer models. Transcriptomic analysis
reveals activation of immune response-related pathways, supporting the multistage
immune activation mechanism.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s commendation on our study.
Weaknesses and Suggestions for Improvement:
- The nano material design of hydrogel and RBCs is less innovative, which has been
reported a lot. It is unclear why the research focuses on CTLA-4 and IL-12, why not
PD-1/PD-L1 and other cytokines?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable questions. Despite the fact that hydrogels
and RBCs have been reported a lot in previous studies, both of them in our research
have been innovatively renovated and engineered for extended applications. In this
study, we innovatively devise an in situ self-assembled hydrogel based on the strategic
introduction of sodium alginate (Alg) and barium dioxide (BaO ). Once injected into
2
the tumor, the acidity-responsive BaO can degrade into Ba2+, which rapidly reacts with
2
biocompatible Alg to form an in situ self-assembled cell reservoir crosslinked network
in the acidic tumor microenvironment rather than neutral normal tissues, thus realizing
effective multidrug encapsulation that is not equipped by traditional hydrogels slowly
chelating with intrinsic metal ions in the body[1]. Besides, the concurrently generated
H O can be catalyzed into O by the catalase (CAT) intrinsic on RBCs, thereby
2 2 2
collectively achieving Ba/O self-compensated radiosensitization.
vitro production, have garnered considerable attraction as an intelligent drug delivery
system[2]. Different from traditional strategies for encapsulating a single drug within
RBCs [3], we innovatively develop a multisite-fettering approach to entrap aCTLA-4 in
the interior and anchor IL-12 on the membrane. Notably, the optimized “alternate
hypotonic and hypertonic dialysis” method is elaborately introduced to encapsulate
aCTLA-4 with both the structural integrity and enzyme activity of RBCs into account.
Beyond being a dual-cargo carrier, those engineered RBCs with preserved CAT
bioactivity can catalyze the production of O from H O for radiosensitization. Overall,
2 2 2
the material design of hydrogel and RBCs is much more innovative than simple in situ
compartmental encapsulation of multiple cargos and can realize sequential aCTLA-
4/IL-12 release for multistage antitumor immune responses without biosafety concerns.
Due to the differential RT sensitivity among immune cells, RT causes a direct
decrease in the ratio of cytotoxic T cells to regulatory T cells (Tregs), accompanied by
the upregulation of CTLA-4 in the initial stage[4-6]. The elevated CTLA-4 expression
inevitably restrains dendritic cell (DC) migration and antigen presentation, thus greatly
attenuating the therapeutic efficacy of RT. Besides, IL-12, as a critical
immunostimulatory agent in both innate and adaptive immune responses, can promote
the proliferation and enhance the function of NK/T cells to shape an immune-activating
tumor microenvironment[7]. To modulate the multistage immune landscape of RT, we
scrupulously combine aCTLA-4 with IL-12 in a temporal manner, thus compensating
primary immunosuppression and instigating relay immunoactivation during the
multistage of RT, which is also the main reason why we focus on aCTLA-4 and IL-12
instead of PD-1/PD-L1 or other cytokines.
References:
[1] Zhao, Z. et al. Capturing magnesium ions via microfluidic hydrogel microspheres
for promoting cancellous bone regeneration. ACS Nano 15, 13041-13054 (2021).
[2] Liu, H. et al. Red blood cells-derived components as biomimetic functional
materials: Matching versatile delivery strategies based on structure and function. Bioact
Mater 47, 481-501 (2025).
[3] Li, Y. et al. Clinical progress and advanced research of red blood cells based drug

[4] Wirsdörfer, F. et al. Combining Radiotherapy and Immunotherapy in Lung Cancer:

[5] Qu, Y. et al. 2-Gy whole-body irradiation significantly alters the balance of
CD4+CD25- T effector cells and CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ T regulatory cells in mice. Cell
Mol Immunol 7, 419-427 (2010).
[6] Persa, E. et al. The effect of ionizing radiation on regulatory T cells in health and

[7] Zou, Z. et al. Anti-PD-1 cis-delivery of low-affinity IL-12 activates intratumoral

- Mechanism of Action: While the authors propose a mechanism for the multistage
immune response, further studies are needed to validate this mechanism. For example,
experiments could be conducted to investigate the timing and kinetics of aCTLA-4 and
IL-12 release, as well as their respective effects on immune cell populations and
function.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s constructive advice. To investigate the timing and
kinetics of aCTLA-4 and IL-12 release, IL-12 and aCTLA-4 were jointly entrapped in
RBCs to obtain IL&aC@RBAH as control. The release behaviors of IL-12 and aCTLA-
4 from IL&aC@RBAH and IL/aC@RBAH in the mildly acidic environment (pH 6.5)
were investigated. As expected, both IL-12 and aCTLA-4 in IL&aC@RBAH were
released rapidly in a similar trend within 48 h (Fig. R1), possibly due to the simple
diffusion of the mixture of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 from the formed pores on RBCs.
Contrarily, IL/aC@RBAH presented a sequential release behavior with rapid release of
approximately 40% aCTLA-4 from the oxygen-induced pores on the RBC membrane
within 48 h and slow release of less than 20% IL-12 from the enlarged channels in the
crosslinked network of the degrading hydrogel within 48 h. Collectively, all those
results affirmed the sequential timing and kinetics of aCTLA-4 and IL-12 release from
IL/aC@RBAH, thus building the foundation for the multistage initiation of immune
responses in vivo.
Fig. R1 Release profiles of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 from IL&aC@RBAH and
IL/aC@RBAH at pH 6.5 within 48 h. n = 3, mean ± SD.
Notably, in our initial submission, we investigated the respective effects of IL-12
and aCTLA-4 on systemic immune responses, as presented in Figs. 5j-r. Herein, to
further unveil the impact of sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 release on the multistage
immune effects, we investigated the immune cell populations in orthotopic 4T1 tumor-
bearing mice exposed to different treatments. Briefly, the orthotopic 4T1-tumor bearing
mice were randomly divided into 5 groups and then respectively treated with saline, RT,
RT + IL-aC (IL-12 prior to aCTLA-4), RT + IL&aC (the mixture of IL-12 and aCTLA-
4), and RT + aC-IL (IL-12 subsequent to aCTLA-4). Compared to the slight
upregulation of CD8+ T cells induced by RT-mediated immunogenic cell death (ICD),
the intratumoral level of those cells was moderately upregulated in the RT + IL-aC and
RT + IL&aC groups (Figs. R2a, b), demonstrating the modest immune activation in the
primary and relay stages. This limitation was likely attributed to the rapid diffusion and
loss of IL-12 from tumor, which was insufficient to sustain downstream activation
during the relay stage. Of note, the RT + aC-IL treatment elicited the utmost increase in
CD8+ T cells, along with the lowest Treg ratio and the highest NK cell level among all
the groups (Figs. R2c, d), indicating the strongest antitumor immune initiation by the
sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 supply parallel to IL/aC@RBAH. Moreover, the IFN-γ
production in CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, and NK cells in the RT + aC-IL group were
all at the highest level among all the groups (Figs. R2e-g), further affirming the most
potent immune responses through aCTLA-4-mediated primary immunosuppression
alleviation and relay IL-12-induced immunoactivation. It is noteworthy that the RT +
aC-IL treatment likewise elicited the uppermost level of mature DCs, which was almost
1.44- and 1.27-fold higher than that in the RT + IL-aC and RT + IL&aC groups (Figs.
R2h, i). The result further elucidated the most powerful antigen-presenting initiation of
the sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 supply in the RT + aC-IL treatment for antitumor
immunity through the DC cell-intrinsic IL-12/IFN-γ positive feedback loop.
Fig. R2 a, b Representative flow cytometry plots (a) and quantification (b) of cytotoxic
T lymphocytes (CD8+ in CD45+CD3+ cells) in orthotopic 4T1 tumors after different
treatments. c, d Quantitative analyses of Tregs (CD4+CD25+ in CD45+CD3+ cells) (c)
and NK cells (CD3-CD49b+ in CD45+ cells) (d) in orthotopic 4T1 tumors after different

Given the intratumoral immune responses elicited by RT + aC-IL, the impacts of
sequential cytokine supply on antigen presentation process were further investigated
through the immune cell populations in the tumor-draining lymph nodes (TDLNs) of
orthotopic 4T1-tumor bearing mice subjected to different treatments. Both the levels of
CD8+ T cell infiltration and activation were at the peak in the RT + aC-IL group (Figs.
R3a-d). Meanwhile, the amounts of both cDC1 and cDC2 to TDLNs were maximally
elevated in the RT + aC-IL group, quite different from those in the other groups (Figs.
R3e, f), further demonstrating the supreme antitumor initiation by the sequential
aCTLA-4/IL-12 supply. Overall, all the results firmly affirmed the virtues of systemic
multistage immune responses induced by the sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 release from
RT + IL/aC@RBAH. We have included Fig. R1 as Supplementary Fig. 33, Figs. R2b-
g and Fig. R2i as Figs. 6e-k, Fig. R3c as Supplementary Fig. 34 and Figs. R3d-f as
Figs. 6l-n. Relevant description has been added in the revised manuscript.
Fig. R3 a Representative flow cytometry plots of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ in
CD45+CD3+ cells) in TDLNs of orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice post different
treatments. b Representative flow cytometry plots of activated CD8+ T lymphocytes
(CD69+ in CD3+CD8+ cells) in TDLNs of orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice post
different treatments. c-f Quantitative analyses of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ in
CD45+CD3+ cells) (c), activated CD8+ T lymphocytes (CD69+ in CD3+CD8+ cells) (d),
cDC1 (CD103+ in CD11c+MHC Ⅱ+ cells) (e) and cDC2 (CD11b+ in CD11c+MHC Ⅱ+
cells) (f) in TDLNs of orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice post different treatments.
Data in c-f were presented as mean ± SD. n = 3 biologically independent samples in c-
f. P values were calculated via student’s t-test.
- Comparison with Other Therapies: The paper would benefit from a direct comparison
with other RT and immunotherapy combinations, including those using different
aCTLA-4 and IL-12 formulations and delivery methods. This would provide a clearer
understanding of the advantages and limitations of the proposed approach.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s helpful suggestions. In this study, we develop an
in situ self-assembled cell reservoir hydrogel to initiate multistage radioimmunotherapy.
Distinct from the simple combination of RT with aCTLA-4 or IL-12 in the previous
studies[1, 2], the proposed approach of RT + IL/aC@RBAH enhances radiosensitivity
and realizes chronologically augmented antitumor immune responses. Specifically, the
designed IL/aC@RBAH can provide a Ba2+ depot and initiate O production for Ba/O
2 2
dual-compensated radiosensitization. Distinguished from the traditional delivery of a
simple cytokine mixture or the sequential local administration of aCTLA-4 and IL-12,
the in situ IL-12/aCTLA-4 multisite-fettering system (IL/aC@RBAH) could facilitate
the sequential release of aCTLA-4 and IL-12 via a single administration (Fig. R1),
thus eliciting multistage antitumor immunity for effective tumor regression (Figs. R2,
R3).
On the other hand, recombinant IL-12 has failed in clinical trials, owing to the
uncontrolled cytokine release syndrome and liver damage[3]. The systemic delivery of
IL-12 by novel nanoparticles has been recently reported a lot, but the potential toxicity
still exists with elevated IL-12 concentration in the serum[4]. Moreover, aCTLA-4 alone
exhibits grade 3-4 immune-related serious side effects (irAEs) in about 54% of patients,
which greatly limits its clinical use[5, 6]. In this study, leveraging the rapid in situ
formation and dilatory degradation of the IL/aC@RBAH hydrogel, aCTLA-4 and IL-
12 can be steadily and slowly released in the tumors, thus avoiding the potential
cytokine storm and the toxicity of free aCTLA-4 and IL-12 to liver damage and kidney
injury (Figs. 4d-i).
Overall, the therapeutic modality of RT + IL/aC@RBAH compensates for the
shortcomings of other RT and immunotherapy combinations by minimizing off-target
effects and reversing RT-induced periodical tumor immunosuppression. In the future,
the self-assembled reservoir hydrogel is promising to be a generic platform to offer
physical support for diverse engineered cells with compartmentalized encapsulation of

cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and oral carcinoma. Moreover, given the
predominant clinical use of RT as a local treatment, the in situ cell reservoir hydrogel
combined with RT in the study holds great potential in ameliorating multistage
antitumor immune responses for effective tumor eradication. With respect to superficial
tumors like skin or oral cancers, percutaneous hydrogel injection can facilitate in situ
rapid formation, followed by localized RT to suppress tumor progression. In cases of
deeper-seated malignancies like pancreatic cancer or prostate cancers, the hydrogel can
be precisely administered via minimally invasive surgery approaches to directly inhibit
tumorigenesis or be deemed to be an adjuvant therapy to prevent postoperative
recurrence. In the future, this designed hydrogel will open new therapeutic avenues in
the application of deeper tumors like hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, and
colon cancer through the integration of precise localized delivery and advanced
interventional techniques. Relevant discussions have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript.

Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s helpful comments. The cancer-immunity cycle is
a multi-step biological process comprising several key stages, including antigen release
from dying tumor cells, antigen presentation, priming and activation of immune cells,
immune cell trafficking and infiltration, and the final tumor recognition and
elimination[1]. Given the multi-step nature of the cancer-immunity cycle, multiplexed
cytokines targeting the immune pathways in different stages need to be developed to
temporally coordinate combinational immunotherapy for enhanced antitumor
responses. In our study, the meticulous design of sequential aCTLA-4 and IL-12 release
is introduced to significantly enhance the antitumor immune efficacy and guarantee the
biosafety of the treatment regime. Briefly, aCTLA-4 primarily promotes the antigen
presentation phase by specifically blocking immune checkpoint molecules CTLA-4 on
T cells. Subsequently, IL-12 enhances the immune effects in the relay stage by
potentiating the function of NK cells, CD8+ T cells, and CD4+ T cells to promote IFN-
γ secretion for boosted tumoricidal activities.
To further broaden its therapeutic applications, future studies may be focused on
combining the current regimen with agents targeting other phases of the cancer-
immunity cycle. On the one side, ICD inducers, such as radiotherapy or anthracycline-
based chemotherapeutic agents, could be incorporated to amplify tumor antigen
release[2]. On the other side, immune cell chemoattractants, including CXCL9 and
CXCL10, might be co-administered to facilitate the infiltration of peripherally primed
T cells into tumor tissues[3]. Additionally, immune adjuvants like Toll-like receptor
agonists could be utilized to prompt intratumoral antigen-presentation, thereby further
potentiating antitumor immune responses[4]. Those multi-pronged combinatorial
approaches would systematically optimize each critical step of the cancer-immunity
cycle for superior antitumor immune outcomes. The pertinent discussion has been
supplemented in the revised manuscript.

Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s insightful comments. The therapeutic system in
our study is composed of RBC modified with dual cargos, barium peroxide, and sodium
alginate. Economically, the engineered RBCs exhibit distinct advantages[1], including
wide availability, high prevalence, and low-cost chemical modification. Additionally,
modified RBCs maintain stable morphological properties for up to 42 days at 2-6 °C[2],
facilitating convenient storage and transportation. Moreover, the barium peroxide
(BaO ) is synthesized via a hydrolytic precipitation method, which also offers the
2
advantages of low cost and economical production[3]. However, BaO exhibits limited
2
stability in deionized water (Fig. 2k), necessitating storage in alcoholic solvents or
suitable preservation systems for transportation and long-term storage, with immediate
preparation preceding therapeutic administration. Moreover, sodium alginate exhibits
excellent potential as a biomaterial due to its high structural stability, mature production
processes, and wide availability from brown algae (e.g., laminaria japonica, lessonia,
etc.)[4]. This low-cost material offers convenient transportability and superior economic
benefits. In this study, alginate-based hydrogels, featuring low production costs and
FDA-approved excellent biocompatibility[5], illuminate a promising feasibility for
clinical translation.
In this study, aCTLA-4 was successfully loaded into RBCs to generate aC@RBC
via hypotonic dialysis, which is a well-established method benefiting from existing
automatic loading instruments, thereby reducing production costs and enhancing
clinical translation potential. Subsequently, IL-12 was anchored onto the surface of
RBCs through membrane insertion to yield IL/aC@RBC, which maintained structural
integrity after 7-day storage at 4 °C (Supplementary Fig. 4), indicating suitability for
extended transportation and storage. However, the membrane insertion approach faces
three critical limitations, involving high-cost lipid reagents, suboptimal antibody
conjugation efficiency, and low insertion efficiency of lipid-conjugated antibodies, thus
contributing to high production costs and operational complexity. Therefore, further
methodology optimization and automatic production system development of the
membrane insertion approach are in demand for clinical translation.
Collectively, the elaborately designed self-assembled hydrogel is a facile platform
with comprehensive economic and logistical considerations. Following the reviewer’s
kind suggestions, we have included relevant discussion in the revised manuscript to
propel its clinical translation.

- Will local RT treatment and/or ROS damage the gel structure? If so, how could cargo
burst release be avoided?
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s constructive questions. Mechanistically, the stable
network structure of the gel is constructed on the covalent cross-linking between Ba2+
and Alg, which is inherently not a ROS-sensitive linkage. Moreover, the RT treatment
could not induce the pore formation on RBC membrane (Fig. R16), suggesting minimal
impact on the aCTLA-4 release kinetics from IL/aC@RBAH. To validate the
assumption, the release profiles of aCTLA-4 and IL-12 from IL/aC@RBAH were
investigated. Similar to those in the mildly acidic environment (pH 6.5) without the RT
treatment, aCTLA-4 and IL-12 in IL/aC@RBAH at pH 6.5 with the RT treatment
likewise showed sequential release behaviors within 48 h (Fig. R17). Notably, nearly
40% of aCTLA-4 was rapidly released from IL/aC@RBAH within 48 h with or without
the RT treatment. Besides, IL-12 in IL/aC@RBAH with or without the RT treatment
also showed a similar release behavior, thus evidencing the effective anchorage on RBC,
as well as the excellent stability of the hydrogel under RT irradiation. Consequently, it
could be concluded that the RT treatment could not disrupt the aCTLA-4 release
through the O -induced pores on RBC membrane while showing negligible impact on
2

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The revised manuscript presents several significant advancements:
1. Sequential Immune Activation: The authors demonstrate a clear sequential release profile of aCTLA-4 (40% within 48 h) followed by IL-12 (<20% over 48 h) from the hydrogel, enabling multistage immune modulation. This is supported by enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration, reduced Treg ratios, and elevated IFN-γ production in the RT+aC-IL group.
2. Ba/O₂ Dual Compensation: The hydrogel’s ability to generate O₂ via CAT-catalyzed H2O2 decomposition and sustain hypoxia alleviation is well-validated, partially addressing a key limitation of radiotherapy.
3. Long-Term Biosafety: Comprehensive toxicity studies and biodistribution data confirm minimal systemic leakage of BaO₂ or RBCs, with no significant organ damage over 2 months.
However, the authors have the following points to consider further:
1. Inadequate Comparison to Current Standards: No comparison to anti-PD1/L1 therapies; Limited data on how the hydrogel outperforms conventional CTLA-4/IL-12 combotherapy.
2. Expand Toxicity Discussion: Include potential immune cell exhaustion risks from prolonged IL-12 exposure.
3. Mechanistic Evidence: While Fig. R16 (Supplementary Fig. 11) shows O₂-induced RBC pore formation, direct visualization of pore dynamics (e.g., time-lapse microscopy) would strengthen the mechanism.
4. Overly Complex System with Limited Clinical Feasibility: The multi-component hydrogel system (RBCs + BaO₂ + Alginate + dual cytokines) introduces significant manufacturing and quality control challenges that undermine translational potential.
While the authors demonstrate proof-of-concept in mice, scaling up engineered RBC production while maintaining batch-to-batch consistency for human trials remains unaddressed. The requirement for intratumoral injection further limits applicability to deep-seated or metastatic tumors.
These comments don't invalidate the work but highlight areas requiring substantial strengthening before the approach could be considered competitive with existing radioimmunotherapy strategies. The authors should address these limitations through additional experiments and more balanced discussion of clinical constraints.

1. Sequential Immune Activation: The authors demonstrate a clear sequential release
profile of aCTLA-4 (40% within 48 h) followed by IL-12 (<20% over 48 h) from the

CD8+ T cell infiltration, reduced Treg ratios, and elevated IFN-γ production in the
RT+aC-IL group.
2. Ba/O₂ Dual Compensation: The hydrogel’s ability to generate O₂ via CAT-catalyzed
H O decomposition and sustain hypoxia alleviation is well-validated, partially
2 2
addressing a key limitation of radiotherapy.
3. Long-Term Biosafety: Comprehensive toxicity studies and biodistribution data
confirm minimal systemic leakage of BaO₂ or RBCs, with no significant organ damage
over 2 months.

However, the authors have the following points to consider further:
1. Inadequate Comparison to Current Standards: No comparison to anti-PD1/L1
therapies; Limited data on how the hydrogel outperforms conventional CTLA-4/IL-12
combotherapy.
Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s valuable comments. Following the reviewer’s
kind suggestions, the respective administrations of anti-PD-1 (aPD-1) and anti-PD-L1
(aPD-L1) in combination with RT were included as standard-of-care (SoC) control
groups for a comprehensive evaluation of the therapeutic efficacy of RT +
IL/aC@RBAH. The orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were randomly allocated into
4 groups and treated with saline, RT + aPD-1, RT + aPD-L1, and RT + IL/aC@RBAH.
Distinct from the rapid tumor progression in the saline group, the tumor volumes in the
RT + aPD-1 and RT + aPD-L1 groups were moderately suppressed (Figs. R1a-c),
indicating the deficient antitumor efficacy of RT combined with immune checkpoint
blockade (ICB) therapy. Intriguingly, the RT + IL/aC@RBAH treatment showed much
more prominent tumor inhibition than the RT + aPD-1 and RT + aPD-L1 groups, thus
illustrating the superior antitumor efficacy of RT + IL/aC@RBAH-mediated multistage
RIT over RT combined with ICB therapy. To further elucidate the underlying immune
mechanisms, we compared the immune effects of RT + IL/aC@RBAH with RT + aPD-
1 and RT + aPD-L1 therapies by assessing immune cell populations in orthotopic 4T1
tumor-bearing mice after different treatments. Relative to the moderate changes in
immune cell levels observed with RT + aPD-1 and RT + aPD-L1, RT + IL/aC@RBAH
markedly increased CD8⁺ T cells and NK cells infiltration while reducing intratumoral
Tregs, thereby enhancing the effector-to-suppressor balance in the tumor
microenvironment (TME) (Figs. R1d-f). Taken together, these results indicate that RT
synergized with the sequential release of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 is superior over its
combination with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 in priming and amplifying antitumor immunity and
in reshaping the TME toward an effector-dominant state that favors immune-mediated
antitumor efficacy.

bioluminescence quantification (b) of orthotopic 4T1-luciferase (4T1-luc) tumor-
bearing mice after treated with saline, RT + aPD-1, RT + aPD-L1, and RT +
IL/aC@RBAH, respectively. c Average tumor growth curves of orthotopic 4T1 tumor-
bearing mice subjected to different treatments. d-f Quantitative analyses of cytotoxic T
lymphocytes (CD8+ in CD45+CD3+ cells) (d), NK cells (CD3-CD49b+ in CD45+ cells)
(e) and Tregs (CD4+CD25+ in CD45+CD3+ cells) (f) in orthotopic 4T1 tumors after
different treatments. Data in b-f were presented as mean ± SD. n = 5 biologically
independent samples in b, c. n = 3 biologically independent samples in d-f. Statistical
significance was determined using two-way ANOVA (b, c). Statistical significance was
determined using student’s t-test in (d-f).
Notably, our initial submission demonstrated that RT + IL/aC@RBAH achieved
superior therapeutic efficacy over conventional aCTLA-4/IL-12 combination therapy,
as presented in Supplementary Fig. 35. Herein, to further elucidate how the hydrogel
outperformed conventional aCTLA-4/IL-12 combination therapy, we investigated the

2. Expand Toxicity Discussion: Include potential immune cell exhaustion risks from

Response: Thanks for the reviewer’s constructive advice. Short-term antigenic or
inflammatory exposure prompts immune cells to undergo memory differentiation,
whereas persistent stimulation drives them toward an exhausted phenotype. Immune
cell exhaustion is characterized by diminished effector function and increased
inhibitory receptor expression, which is associated with detrimental drug resistance[1, 2].
Studies have shown that key cytokines driving immune cell exhaustion in vivo include
IL-10, IFN-I, TGF-β, and IL-23, while IL-12 often acts to reverse or alleviate the
exhaustion in the majority of settings[3-6]. Despite its generally restorative role in the
immune recovery, sustained intratumoral IL-12 exposure at a high level from the
hydrogel might paradoxically promote immune cell exhaustion, accompanied by
heightened metabolic demand and increased susceptibility to activation-induced
dysfunction. Nevertheless, the critical driving factor of exhaustion remains persistent
antigen exposure[7]. By rapidly suppressing tumor growth and thereby markedly
reducing the antigen exposure of intratumoral immune cells, RT + IL/aC@RBAH is
expected to prevent immune cell exhaustion, thereby outweighing any potential IL-12-
associated pro-exhaustion effect. In the revised manuscript, we explicitly
acknowledged the possibility of immune cell exhaustion under sustained IL-12, and
discussed that limited dose intensity and exposure duration could reduce this risk.
Relevant description has been added in the revised manuscript.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Radiotherapy (RT) is a clinical mainstay of cancer treatment that triggers tumor-specific immune responses. However, the effectiveness is usually hampered due to the hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME) and the ambivalent impact of RT on the immune landscape of tumors. Herein, we develop an injectable hydrogel encapsulating interleukin-12 (IL-12)/anti-CTLA-4 (aCTLA-4) co-engineered red blood cells (RBC), which is in situ self-assembled within the TME to increase oxygen supply and instigate sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 release, thus achieving Ba/O2 self-compensated radiosensitization and activating multistage immune responses. Once in the acidic TME, the in situ injected BaO2 undergoes hydrolysis to generate H2O2 and Ba2+, followed by the rapid reaction of Ba2+ with sodium alginate to afford a biocompatible hydrogel. Meanwhile, catalase presented on RBC converts H2O2 into O2, thereby alleviating hypoxia-induced radioresistance and inducing O2-mediated pore formation on RBC membrane for rapid release of aCTLA-4 to relieve tumor immunosuppression. Subsequently, IL-12 anchored on RBC is dilatorily released and interacts with T/NK cells within the TME to induce IFN-γ-dependent antitumor immunity. Taken together, the in situ self-assembled cell reservoir hydrogel offers a futuristic avenue to realize multistage radioimmunotherapy for effective tumor regression by programmable immunoregulation with significant clinical value.

---

## Introduction

Radiotherapy (RT) is a prominent clinical treatment modality for cancer by focusing a local beam of radiation at the tumor site1,2. Extensive investigations have recently revealed its dual natures in provoking DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in tumor cells as well as eliciting the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs)3, thereby promoting the recruitment and maturation of dendritic cells (DCs) by instigating systemic antitumor immunity4. Of note, the effectiveness of RT is often restricted by tumor hypoxia5, which competitively reduces the DNA radicals (DNA·) to produce DNA-OO·6,7, thus resulting in less damage fixation and decreased DSBs. Moreover, due to the differential RT sensitivity among immune cells, RT may cause a direct decrease in the ratio of cytotoxic T cells to regulatory T cells (Tregs)8, accompanied by the upregulation of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4)9. This inevitably restrains the DC migration and inhibits the transportation of tumor antigens to tumor-draining lymph nodes (TDLNs)10, thus greatly attenuating the therapeutic efficacy of RT. Consequently, it is a pressing priority to explore unparalleled combinational therapeutic approaches to increase intratumoral oxygen supply and alleviate tumor immunosuppression for ameliorating therapeutic outcomes of RT.

Cancer immunotherapy has been extensively investigated as a vital part of recent advent and revolutionized the profound outlook through immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) strategies11. Anti-CTLA-4 (aCTLA-4) serves as an immune modulator to inhibit CTLA-4 function12,13, thus dampening the activity of Tregs while simultaneously promoting DC maturation and even facilitating the migration of both cDC1 and cDC2 to TDLNs for CD8+ T and CD4+ T cells activation14,15. In recent years, significant research interests have been attracted to the concurrent administration of aCTLA-4 with RT to harness the potential synergism between the two treatment modalities16. Despite promising preclinical results and substantial mechanism evidence of the synergism, a majority of studies at the clinical level fail to verify the positive effect of the combined treatments17, possibly due to the simple immune checkpoint blockade insufficient to relieve cytotoxic T cell depletion and NK cell exhaustion within the TME18. Interleukin-12 (IL-12), a crucial immune cytokine, emerges as a pivotal immunostimulatory agent capable of stimulating both the innate and adaptive immune systems19. As one of the direct downstream molecules of IL-12, IFN-γ, secreted by natural killer (NK) and T cells20, promotes the recruitment of immune cells into tumors as well as instigates the DC cell-intrinsic IL-12/IFN-γ positive feedback loop21, thus bolstering antitumor responses via immune engine refueling. Hence, the integrated utilization of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 exhibits immense potential in augmenting antitumor efficacy by synergistic combination with RT22. Nevertheless, a major concern arises from the direct injection of the mixture of IL-12 and aCTLA-4 (IL/aC), which may result in uncontrolled activation of immune cells and an IL-12-induced cytokine storm23. Therefore, we postulate that orchestrating an in situ IL-12/aCTLA-4 multisite-fettering system could be a promising strategy to facilitate the application of dual immunostimulatory agents in combination with RT, thereby maximizing antitumor responses while minimizing adverse effects.

Hydrogels, defined as water-swollen and insoluble three-dimensional (3D) crosslinked networks similar to the tumor extracellular matrix24, can offer physical support for engineered cells and slow release of loaded cargos25, thus holding great potential in enabling long-term therapeutic effects and efficient tumor intervention. In comparison to synthetic hydrogels, natural hydrogels exhibit superior biodegradability26 and unexceptionable biocompatibility27, which are advantageous for applications requiring high biological compatibility and environmental sustainability. Sodium alginate (Alg), a natural polymer that remains stable within the biological environment, bears a strong resemblance to the extracellular matrix28, thus demonstrating low immunogenicity and excellent biocompatibility29. Furthermore, Alg can be degraded into nontoxic polysaccharides that do not participate in normal metabolic processes30,31. Due to the multiple merits of this natural polymer discussed above, Alg-based hydrogel is a potentially attractive alternative as a drug-encapsulating depot with negligible biosafety concerns32,33. However, traditional Alg-based hydrogels generally chelate with metal ions intrinsic in the body and lack precise control over the architecture formation34, which may result in drug leakage and potential toxicity. Hence, the development of a TME-responsive in situ-formed Alg-based hydrogel emerges as an urgent demand for spatiotemporally controlled drug release and unleashed antitumor efficacy.

In this study, we devise an in situ self-assembled cell reservoir crosslinked network based on the introduction of barium dioxide (BaO2) into the synthesis of injectable hydrogels with locoregional delivery of IL-12/aCTLA-4 co-engineered red blood cells (IL-12/aCTLA-4@RBC-BaO2-Alg hydrogel, IL/aC@RBAH) to initiate multistage immune effects for amplified synergistic radioimmunotherapy (RIT) (Fig. 1). Upon intratumoral injection of the hydrogel precursors, BaO2 undergoes rapid hydrolysis within the acidic TME to release H2O2 and Ba2+, which quickly reacts with Alg to form hydrogels to entrap multiple cargos within the TME. Simultaneously, the generated H2O2 is decomposed under the catalysis of catalase (CAT) presented on RBC to produce oxygen for endogenous O2 furnishment. This multifaceted process not only alleviates tumor hypoxia-induced radioresistance, but also triggers pore formation on RBC membrane (RBCM) for rapid release of aCTLA-4. Subsequently, IL-12 anchored on RBC initiates activation of cytotoxic T/NK cells in the TME, with mitigated potential immunotoxicity by the immobilization on RBC surface and steady in situ retention of the hydrogel. The sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 releasing hydrogel unleashes a therapeutic window in step wise modulating immune networks, signified by significantly enhanced DC homing, boosted antitumor T cell infiltration, and NK cell recruitment for garnering an immunostimulatory TME. Notably, the synergy between Ba/O2 dual-compensated RT and sequential aCTLA-4/IL-12 release potentiates a benefit in both innate and adaptive immune activation to reshape the immune landscape of the TME and bolster the attack on both poorly immunogenic 4T1 triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and Panc02 pancreatic cancer. Collectively, the meticulous design of engineered RBC-encapsulating hydrogels offers a facile and feasible approach to synergize radiotherapy with immunotherapy to garner multistage radioimmunotherapy for reinvigored antitumor immune responses and effective tumor regression.
